A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UnSeenTimeQA. Their main text, tables, figures and appendices are readable and can be matched reliably. v4 retains Appendices A–F and adds Appendix G.

before.justification: v3 reports original GPT-4 context-alteration experiments, evaluations of five LLMs on UnSeenTimeQA, few-shot experiments in Appendix B, and depth and error analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains these original empirical results and adds human question-answering results in Tables 2 and 3.

M1.justification: The logistics-plan generation, event durations, templates, event tracking, answer construction and LLM prompting remain substantively unchanged. Section 4.4 explains linked-event timelines more explicitly, while on-demand generation is newly emphasized without specifying a different generation algorithm.

E1.justification: v4 removes TempReason's Time-Time task from Tables 1 and 4, retaining its Event-Time and Event-Event tasks. The remaining benchmark coverage and UnSeenTimeQA's logistics domain, four difficulty categories and three question types remain unchanged. Appendix G's suggested additional uses are not evaluated.

E2.justification: Tables 2 and 3 add a Human comparator alongside the same five LLMs. This comparison is distinct from the web-search reviewers already present in v3. The model comparator sets in the existing zero-shot and few-shot experiments are unchanged.

E3.justification: The new human evaluation uses three reviewers and 15 questions per difficulty level. Section 3 and Appendix A.1 revise the existing-benchmark sample total from 1,650 to 1,500, although Table 4's caption retains 1,650. Appendix D revises serial delay instructions from subsequent dependent events to all subsequent events. Section 7 drops 'each' from the 60-error sampling description, leaving allocation between hard conditions ambiguous; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 removes the quantitative context-alteration consistency check of seven inconsistencies among 100 samples, retaining only the description 'negligible.' Section 6 also omits the statement that similar depth trends occur for easy and medium questions. The plotted depth analysis, few-shot comparisons and four-category error analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report LLM mean accuracy and standard deviation across three sampled data splits in Tables 2, 3, 5 and 6. No changed repetition counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. The new human rows provide mean accuracy across three reviewers without introducing uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v4 adds human average accuracies of 100% for easy and medium, 93.33% for hard serial, and 84.44% for hard parallel in Tables 2–3. It removes TempReason Time-Time's 97% no-context result and the seven-in-100 inconsistency finding. Retained LLM scores, including Appendix B's few-shot results, are unchanged. Human results use smaller subsets, so they are not matched-sample performance improvements.

T1.justification: The depth definition and underlying temporal-reasoning framework remain unchanged. Neither version introduces theorems, proofs or mathematical derivations. Clarifications of the already-serial examples do not establish a new formal model.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction newly identify on-demand question generation through an open-source framework as a contribution and explain its role in avoiding stale evaluation data. The central claims about synthetic TSQA, sequential and parallel events, and LLM reasoning weaknesses are retained.

C2.justification: v4 interprets the new human results as evidence of a human–LLM performance gap and expands the explanation of how fresh synthetic questions address future contamination. Appendix G suggests applications such as timeline reconstruction and temporal relationship extraction. The existing limitations concerning temporal range, templates, answerability and English remain.

D1.justification: v4 substantially expands benchmark access and reuse documentation: it adds code/data repository and dataset-host links, states public availability, and supplies Appendix G with licensing, provenance, maintenance and version-retention information. Section 4.4 and Appendix G newly disclose iterative manual validation and Python-based generation. Existing prompt, model-endpoint and GPU details remain. These are documentation disclosures; the PDFs do not establish when the linked resources became accessible.

R1.justification: v4 adds Gebru et al. (2021), Datasheets for Datasets, to support Appendix G. It also emphasizes on-demand generation in its positioning against benchmarks vulnerable to future contamination. The substantive related-work survey and existing benchmark citations are otherwise retained.

P1.justification: v4 expands and rewrites portions of the introduction, context-alteration explanation and event-tracking description, renames Section 3's subsections around knowledge cut-off dates, and adds acknowledgments and a datasheet appendix. These are localized narrative revisions; the existing section sequence and extensive example appendix remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v4 adds a contamination schematic as Figure 1, inserts human rows and expands captions in Tables 2–3, and removes the Time-Time rows from Tables 1 and 4. The error-example figure receives label and explanation edits. Existing plots retain their visual content, with figure renumbering and page reflow.

improvement.justification: v4 improves usability through explicit code/data access information and Appendix G, clarifies experimental manipulations, and adds a useful small human reference in Tables 2–3. The gains are limited by sparse human-protocol documentation, the stale sample total in Table 4's caption, and removal of the quantified consistency audit. Overall, documentation and empirical context improve modestly while the main LLM evidence remains unchanged.
